chapter: Later ventures, lodges and San Francisco recollections
title: Make-up bands and the thirty tunes everybody knew
summary: Bands were assembled from whoever was available because everyone knew twenty-five or thirty standards without rehearsal.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: So who were some of the musicians you used to get jobs for--who worked in these bands that you used to put together?
Oh, anyone that was in town or needed around. Sometimes they would have to...it was a make-up band generally always.

A good saxophone player--he knew a piano player, and he'd get...we'd call him, and he'd get a piano player and a drummer and a trumpet... whatever it with. Sometimes some guy'd be playing--if he wasn't working tonight, he'd get on this job. If he wasn't...tomorrow night, if you need him, he'd be on your job. Those days, you know, it wasn't like today. Everybody knew...it was about, what we call 'em--"crips." We called 'em cripples, you know, because you had about thirty tunes that everybody knew--uh, "Alabama Days" and "Maggie, I'm Growin' Old" and all, you know, things like that. You...you'd say, "Now we gonna play 'Maggie'...[hums]-- everybody knew it. And "St. Louis Blues," you know. Everybody knew those things. And you had about twenty tunes or about twenty-five tunes that you never had to rehearse. Everybody knew 'em. So you could get me or anybody else. If you got any late stuff, you give out the music, you know, and maybe you play four...five late songs. All the rest of it...[End of reel].
